subject: literature
passage: For the three years the Okonkwos had lived on Larch Street, Mr. Halloran next door had refused every invitation to dinner, always with the same courteous excuse about his hours at the depot. Still, on most Sunday mornings a loaf of soda bread appeared on their back step, wrapped in a clean cloth and still warm, and when Mrs. Okonkwo's roses failed one spring, a row of cuttings from his own bushes was found planted along her fence before she had so much as mentioned the loss. Mrs. Okonkwo came to understand that her neighbor's refusals ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: were no measure of his regard for her family.
choices.B: concealed a resentment that he could not bring himself to voice.
choices.C: were the reason he had begun leaving the bread in secret.
choices.D: would end as soon as his working hours at the depot changed.

explanation.why: Mr. Halloran declines every invitation, yet he bakes for the family weekly and quietly replaces their lost roses before being asked. Actions this generous cannot come from dislike. The refusals, then, say something about him, perhaps shyness or habit, but nothing about how little he values the family.
explanation.A: Correct. The warm bread and the unasked-for rose cuttings show real goodwill, so the refusals must mean something other than coldness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Weekly gifts of bread and rose cuttings are the acts of a well-wisher, not of someone nursing resentment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never presents the bread as an apology for the refusals; it presents both as parts of the same quiet character.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text treats the hours as an excuse and gives no reason to think the refusals depend on them.
